specPoints.text: know the trends in solubility of the hydroxides and sulfates of Group 2 elements

primer.text: Two solubility arrows point in opposite directions down Group 2: hydroxides dissolve more readily as you descend, while sulfates become stubbornly insoluble. This note quantifies both trends from the data tables and connects hydroxide solubility to the growing alkalinity of oxide-water solutions.

lessons.title: Hydroxide solubility and the alkalinity ladder
sourceHeadings: Solubility of the Group 2 Hydroxides Table
lessons.opening: The oxide-water solutions grow more alkaline downward because the hydroxides themselves dissolve more readily. This lesson quantifies the ladder from Mg(OH)2's 2.0 x 10-5 up to Ba(OH)2's 1.5 x 10-2 moles per 100 g of water.
keyPoints: Dissolved oxides release hydroxide through O2- + H2O -> 2OH-.
The more hydroxide ions a solution holds, the more alkaline it is.
Alkalinity is therefore governed by hydroxide solubility.
Solubility climbs from Mg(OH)2 at 2.0 x 10-5 through Ca(OH)2 and Sr(OH)2 to Ba(OH)2 at 1.5 x 10-2.
Each hydroxide dissolves as X(OH)2 -> X2+ + 2OH-, doubling the ion yield per formula unit.

low.restatement: Solubility sets the hydroxide supply, and the hydroxide supply sets the pH - the table's climb from magnesium to barium is the alkalinity ladder in numbers.
low.analogy: Four taps dripping into one tank, each opening wider than the last: the water level (alkalinity) rises with the tap size (solubility).
low.examPointer: Quote at least two table values when asked to demonstrate the trend - one figure alone cannot show a climb.

medium.restatement: Each formula unit of X(OH)2 releases two OH- ions, so dissolved concentration maps directly onto pH; the 750-fold solubility span from magnesium to barium hydroxide compounds the doubling into a steeprise in alkalinity.
medium.analogy: A pay rise applied twice: first the wage (solubility) climbs, then each employee (formula unit) brings a plus-one (second hydroxide), compounding the household income.
medium.examPointer: The oxide trend and the hydroxide trend are one story - link them explicitly through the OH- concentration in explanations.

check.stem: Which ion's concentration controls how alkaline an oxide-water solution is?

options.explanation: Hydroxide concentration is the alkalinity dial.
The oxide ion is consumed before the solution exists.
The cation rides along, not the driver.
Alkalinity is hydroxide-driven here.

check.stem: Which hydroxide is the least soluble of Group 2 at 298 K?

options.text: Mg(OH)2, at 2.0 x 10-5 mol per 100 g water
options.explanation: The table's smallest entry.
That is the second step up.
That is the maximum.
Third in the climb.

check.stem: How many hydroxide ions does one dissolved formula unit of X(OH)2 release?

options.explanation: The equation X(OH)2 -> X2+ + 2OH- doubles the yield.
The subscript 2 forbids that.
No quadrupling exists.
Dissolution alone releases them.

check.stem: Why does increasing hydroxide solubility raise the pH of the oxide solutions?

options.text: More dissolved hydroxide means a higher OH- concentration and a higher pH
options.explanation: Concentration feeds the pH scale directly.

options.text: pH depends on the cation's identity
options.explanation: The cation is a spectator for pH.
The direction is inverted.
Temperature is fixed at 298 K here.

check.stem: What is the correct trend statement for Group 2 hydroxide solubility?

options.text: It increases going down the group
options.explanation: Magnesium to barium climbs in the table.

options.text: It decreases going down the group
options.explanation: That is the sulfate trend.

options.text: It is constant across the group
options.explanation: The table spans three orders of magnitude.
The climb runs unbroken to barium.

check.stem: Quote the solubility values of Mg(OH)2 and Ba(OH)2 at 298 K.
check.modelAnswer: Mg(OH)2 sits at 2.0 x 10-5 and Ba(OH)2 at 1.5 x 10-2 mol per 100 g of water.

check.stem: Write the dissolution equation of a Group 2 hydroxide.
Explain why the alkalinity trend of oxide solutions mirrors hydroxide solubility.
check.modelAnswer: The oxide's water reaction ends at the hydroxide; whatever controls how much hydroxide dissolves controls the OH- concentration, so the two trends are one trend read from two ends.

check.stem: If Sr(OH)2's solubility is 3.4 x 10-3 mol per 100 g water, what OH- concentration does each dissolved formula unit contribute?
check.modelAnswer: Two hydroxides per formula unit give 6.8 x 10-3 mol of OH- per 100 g of water.

lessons.title: Sulfate solubility and the Group 1 comparison
lessons.opening: The sulfate arrow points the opposite way: solubility collapses down the group until barium sulfate barely dissolves at all. This lesson closes with the Group 1 comparison - why those compounds never precipitate and how barium hydroxide still loses to potassium hydroxide.
keyPoints: The solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases going down the group.
Barium sulfate is effectively insoluble, the classic white precipitate.
Group 1 compounds are all soluble, so they never precipitate in cation tests.
Flame tests, not precipitation, identify Group 1 cations.
Even the most soluble Group 2 hydroxide, Ba(OH)2 at 4.68 g per 100 cm3, loses to KOH at 121 g.

low.restatement: Sulfates sink in solubility as you descend, Group 1 salts never sink at all, and even barium hydroxide's respectable figure cannot match potassium hydroxide's enormous one.
low.analogy: A water slide running the wrong way: Group 2 sulfates slide into shallower pools (less soluble) while Group 1 salts never leave the deep end.
low.examPointer: Bring the numbers: Ba(OH)2 at 4.68 g per 100 cm3 against KOH at 121 g - the comparison proves the 'increases down the group' claim is group-relative only.

medium.restatement: The sulfate descent means each step down trades solubility for lattice strength, ending at BaSO4's near-zero dissolution; the absence of any Group 1 precipitation follows from their universal solubility, which redirects cation testing to flame colours.
medium.analogy: Two opposite escalators in one mall: sulfates descend floor by floor until they stop at the basement (BaSO4), while Group 1 salts ride an up-only escalator with no exit.
medium.examPointer: Answer 'why no Group 1 trends' with 'all soluble, no precipitates, use flame tests' - the three-part answer earns all three marks.

check.stem: Which Group 2 sulfate is effectively insoluble?

options.explanation: The descent bottoms out at barium.
Magnesium sits at the soluble top.
Calcium is mid-trend.
Strontium is second from the bottom.

check.stem: How does Group 2 sulfate solubility trend down the group?

options.explanation: Each step down dissolves less.
That is the hydroxide trend.
BaSO4's insolubility breaks any uniformity.
The descent is monotonic.

check.stem: Why do Group 1 compounds never produce precipitates in cation tests?

options.text: Every Group 1 compound dissolves in water
options.explanation: Universal solubility leaves nothing to precipitate.

options.text: Their ions are too small to precipitate
options.explanation: Size is not the mechanism.

options.text: They react with the test reagents
options.explanation: They simply stay dissolved.

options.text: Precipitation tests exclude alkali metals by rule
options.explanation: The chemistry, not a rule, decides.

check.stem: How are Group 1 cations identified instead?

options.text: By flame tests, using their characteristic colours
options.explanation: Flame colours replace precipitation for the alkali metals.
No precipitate would form to read.
pH cannot distinguish cations.
Flame tests identify them clearly.

check.stem: At 25 degrees C, how does Ba(OH)2's solubility compare with KOH's?

options.text: Ba(OH)2 reaches 4.68 g per 100 cm3 while KOH reaches 121 g
options.explanation: The alkali metal hydroxide outruns the heaviest Group 2 one.

options.text: Ba(OH)2 is more soluble than KOH
options.explanation: The comparison goes the other way.
A 25-fold gap separates them.

options.text: Neither is soluble enough to compare
options.explanation: Both figures are large and comparable.

check.stem: State the sulfate solubility trend down Group 2.
check.modelAnswer: The solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases going down the group.

check.stem: Quote the two solubility figures from the Group 1 comparison.
check.modelAnswer: Ba(OH)2 dissolves 4.68 g per 100 cm3 at 25 degrees C; KOH dissolves 121 g per 100 cm3.

check.stem: Explain why 'Group 2 hydroxide solubility increases down the group' needs the group qualifier.
check.modelAnswer: The claim ranks the hydroxides within Group 2 only; potassium hydroxide's 121 g dwarfs barium hydroxide's 4.68 g, so crossing group lines inverts the comparison.

check.stem: How many times more soluble is KOH than Ba(OH)2 by the quoted figures, to the nearest whole number?
check.modelAnswer: 121 divided by 4.68 is about 26, so potassium hydroxide is roughly 26 times more soluble.

glossary.definition: The increase in Group 2 hydroxide solubility from Mg(OH)2 down to Ba(OH)2 that drives the alkalinity ladder.
The decrease in Group 2 sulfate solubility down the group, bottoming out at insoluble barium sulfate.
The solid observation signalling an insoluble product, as in the barium sulfate test for sulfate ions.
